name: Storytelling frameworks
author: Creator Toolset
description: 21 well-known story, persuasion and argument structures (AIDA, PAS, Story Circle, SCQA, Toulmin…), each with steps, when to use it and a short example.

frameworks.name: Five-Stage Spine
frameworks.pairsWith: Any persuasion formula; Hook – Story – Offer for the ask, Myth – Truth – Proof when the piece argues against a belief.
frameworks.summary: A concrete trigger, proof shown not claimed, the cost of staying the same, a simpler lens, and a takeaway that makes the ask feel inevitable.
steps: Trigger: one concrete moment that breaks an assumption or exposes an irony
Credibility: lived proof or authority shown inside the story, never claimed
Tension: the cost of staying the same — what is at risk if nothing changes
Reframe: a clearer, simpler lens on the problem
Takeaway: the moral insight, then the ask as the next sentence, not a commercial break
frameworks.whenToUse: The skeleton under most persuasive pieces. Emotional arc: calm → curiosity → friction → revelation → conviction. Never end on fear; end on agency.
frameworks.example: A bread that never rises (trigger) → the baker weighs every bag of flour (proof) → the same loaf every week, nothing changes (cost) → the yeast is dead, not the oven (reframe) → fresh yeast is the answer, not the recipe (takeaway).

frameworks.name: AIDA with Story Loops
frameworks.pairsWith: Any narrative shape; Myth – Truth – Proof inside the Interest section.
frameworks.summary: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action — with a loop opened at the top, mini-payoffs inside (set-up, tension, resolution), re-hooks between them, and the loop closed right into the ask.
steps: Attention: a provocative statement that teases the takeaway without giving it away
Interest: open the story loop and deliver a first mini-payoff — set-up, tension, resolution
Desire: raise the stakes; re-hook every few beats by naming the pain again or teasing the next takeaway
Second mini-payoff with the non-obvious value
Action: close the loop by delivering the opening promise, then the ask before it feels like an ending
frameworks.whenToUse: Teaching pieces of any length. The hook opens a loop; nested loops close inner first; never open a loop you don't close.
frameworks.example: "Burning a candle in your living room is basically burning a jar of diesel." → the loop → the mechanism → the fix → one-line ask.

frameworks.name: Two Loops
frameworks.pairsWith: Myth – Truth – Proof for the turn; Hook – Story – Offer or Deliver, Then Tease for the ask.
frameworks.summary: The hook promises two things. The first is answered within seconds, so the viewer knows the piece pays; the second stays open and carries the rest. Before the first answer is explained, a turn says what people get wrong about it.
steps: Hook: promise two things in one line
Answer the first one right away, in a sentence or two
Turn before explaining it: what people get wrong about it, or why it isn't what they'd think
Explain only the part the viewer doesn't already know
Open the second: what it is and what it costs to miss it; each smaller answer opens the next question
Answer the second last, then the ask
frameworks.whenToUse: Teaching pieces where the answer is short and the why is the value: reels, carousels (slide 1 promises two, slide 2 answers the first), long-form chapters. Not for a piece with one point.
frameworks.example: "Two things decide how fast dough rises. The first is temperature." → but not the way most of us do it: the kitchen is colder than we think → what that cold does to the timing → "the second is how long you let it rest" → one thing to check tonight.

frameworks.name: Three-Act Revelation
frameworks.pairsWith: PASTOR or Problem – Agitate – Solve for the close; Myth – Truth – Proof for the investigation act.
frameworks.summary: Setup, investigation, revelation: a grand payoff promised at the start, evidence and mini-reveals layered toward it, then the complete picture and what to do with it.
steps: Setup: a relatable problem, the promise of a transformation, credibility, a first breadcrumb
Investigation: the surprising discovery, validation, personal stakes, mounting evidence, the counterargument handled
Revelation: the final piece falls into place and the complete picture appears
Implementation: exactly what to do, and what life looks like after
Tease the next piece of the puzzle
frameworks.whenToUse: Long-form explainers, deep-dive carousels, essays. Keep 3–5 questions open at once; each answer opens a new one; the payoff must exceed the promise.
frameworks.example: Everyday item → the hidden process → why it's hidden → what it does to you → how to find the real version.

frameworks.name: Backwards Reveal
frameworks.pairsWith: Myth – Truth – Proof (the negated causes are the myths); Promise – Picture – Proof – Push for the push at the end.
frameworks.summary: Lead with the outcome, negate the expected causes, walk the myths one by one, then show what actually worked and why.
steps: The surprising outcome, stated plainly
"And I didn't do any of these things" — negate the causes people expect
The myths, one at a time
What actually made the difference
Why it works
How to apply it at your stage
frameworks.whenToUse: Results-led stories. The negation on the second beat is the most reliable hook-after-the-hook there is.
frameworks.example: Ran my first five kilometres at fifty. And I didn't do any of these five things.

frameworks.name: Pixar Pitch
frameworks.pairsWith: Problem – Agitate – Solve or Before – After – Bridge: the until-one-day beat is the problem, the until-finally beat is the after.
frameworks.summary: Once upon a time, every day, until one day, because of that, until finally — then what it means and one thing to do.
steps: Once upon a time…
Every day…
Until one day…
Because of that… (repeat until the chain is complete)
Until finally…
What it means
One thing to do today
frameworks.whenToUse: Any story with a real turning point. The "every day" beat is where the audience recognises themselves.
frameworks.example: Every day we fill the kettle for the same tea. Until one day the kettle breaks and we find the café down the road does it better.

frameworks.name: Promise – Picture – Proof – Push
frameworks.pairsWith: Backwards Reveal, Three-Act Revelation.
frameworks.summary: A promise, the after painted in sensory detail, proof, proof against the objections, then the push.
steps: Promise: what changes
Picture: the after, in sensory detail — show it, don't argue it
Proof: evidence, numbers, a real example
Proof against the objections they are already forming
Push: the ask
frameworks.whenToUse: Warm audiences and conversion pieces. Show the after, don't sell the before.
frameworks.example: Your loaf on the rack, the crust still crackling, and you already reaching for the knife with both hands.

frameworks.name: I Was Wrong
frameworks.pairsWith: Myth – Truth – Proof (your old belief is the myth); Before – After – Bridge for what you do now.
frameworks.summary: A confident wrong claim, the evidence that broke it, the unfolding told as a witness, a reframe that lands late, and what you do now.
steps: The moment, in a specific time and place
The confident claim you held
The evidence that didn't fit
The unfolding, told as a witness rather than a narrator
The reframe, landing late — not right after the evidence
What you do now
Leave them in the new position — no question back, no invitation to reply
frameworks.whenToUse: The confession arc: personal stories and comment-heavy pieces. Specificity over confession; the lesson lands near the end.
frameworks.example: I was standing in the kitchen at 6:47 in the morning holding a bread manual, certain twenty minutes was nothing.

frameworks.name: Story Circle
frameworks.pairsWith: Monroe's Motivated Sequence for the ask; Myth – Truth – Proof when the 'find' beat overturns a belief.
frameworks.summary: Dan Harmon's eight-step compression of the Hero's Journey: leave comfort for a need, adapt, get it, pay for it, come back changed.
steps: You: a character in a zone of comfort
Need: but they want something
Go: so they enter an unfamiliar situation
Search: adapt to it
Find: get what they wanted
Take: pay a heavy price for it
Return: come back to the familiar situation
Change: having changed
frameworks.whenToUse: Any story with a real journey: a parent's change of mind, a family's routine, a brand origin. The 'take' beat is what most drafts skip.
frameworks.example: Comfortable with the bread machine → wants a loaf that tastes like a bakery → the first class → learning the dough → the rise arrives → the method costs twenty minutes a day → back to normal life → a different baker.

frameworks.name: StoryBrand
frameworks.pairsWith: Promise – Picture – Proof – Push; Before – After – Bridge. The audience is the hero, you are the guide.
frameworks.summary: A brand-story structure named after Donald Miller's StoryBrand, in our words: the viewer is the hero with a want and a problem, you are the guide with a plan, and the piece ends on the ask, the cost of waiting and the result.
steps: The hero: your viewer, and the one thing they want
What stands in the way: the practical problem, how it makes them feel, and why it isn't fair
You step in as the guide: you understand the problem and have solved it
A short, clear plan they can follow
One direct ask: the step to take now
What doing nothing costs them
What life looks like once it works
frameworks.whenToUse: Marketing and brand messaging of any length. Never make yourself the hero; the audience is the hero and you are the guide.
frameworks.example: A cook wants a better stock → jars everywhere, guilt, "this can't be right" → a chef who did the work → a method matched to the week → start tonight → skip the shortcut → a stock worth keeping.

frameworks.name: Kishōtenketsu
frameworks.pairsWith: Myth – Truth – Proof (the twist is where the belief breaks); Backwards Reveal.
frameworks.summary: The four-act East Asian structure with no conflict: introduce, develop, twist, reconcile. The twist recontextualises everything before it.
steps: Ki — introduce: the setting and the people, calmly
Shō — develop: deepen it, no conflict yet
Ten — twist: a new element that recontextualises what came before
Ketsu — reconcile: bring the two together into a conclusion
frameworks.whenToUse: Reveal-driven pieces where the surprise is the point, and audiences tired of manufactured conflict. Works for a carousel as well as a two-minute talk.
frameworks.example: A quiet morning with the same cereal → the same every day, contentedly → a textbook page on what breakfast costs → the morning again, with a real breakfast.

frameworks.name: Monroe's Motivated Sequence
frameworks.pairsWith: Story Circle, Three-Act Revelation, Five-Stage Spine.
frameworks.summary: The classic five-step persuasion sequence for speeches: attention, need, satisfaction, visualisation, action.
steps: Attention: earn it with something specific
Need: the problem, with evidence, and why it touches them
Satisfaction: the solution and how it meets the need
Visualisation: life with the solution, or without it
Action: exactly what to do next
frameworks.whenToUse: Talks, videos, emails and pages that end in one clear action. Visualisation is the beat that separates it from PAS.
frameworks.example: Attention: thirty-one thousand steps a day → need: a day at a desk is a day of none → satisfaction: fifteen minutes outside → visualisation: the first sunny walk → action: tonight.

frameworks.name: SCQA
frameworks.pairsWith: Three-Act Revelation, Backwards Reveal; any persuasion formula for the close.
frameworks.summary: Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle opener: situation, complication, question, answer — then the support beneath the answer.
steps: Situation: what everyone already agrees on
Complication: what changed and made it a problem
Question: the question that raises
Answer: the answer, stated first
Support: the reasons beneath the answer, grouped, strongest first
frameworks.whenToUse: Explainers, memos, long captions, anything that has to argue clearly. The answer comes before the reasons, never after.
frameworks.example: Cooks used to knead by hand all day → now the day is the machine, the timer, the mixer → what does that cost? → the feel of the dough the hands never learn → the three findings behind that.

frameworks.name: Toulmin
frameworks.pairsWith: Any shape; Myth – Truth – Proof when the claim overturns a belief.
frameworks.summary: Stephen Toulmin's anatomy of an argument: claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal. Makes the reasoning inspectable.
steps: Claim: what you are asserting
Grounds: the evidence for it
Warrant: why that evidence supports the claim
Backing: what supports the warrant
Qualifier: how far the claim holds (most, usually, in this age range)
Rebuttal: where it does not hold, said before the audience says it
frameworks.whenToUse: Science-led pieces and anything that will be challenged in the comments. The qualifier and the rebuttal are what make a claim trustworthy.
frameworks.example: Claim: shortcuts ruin the crumb → grounds: the study → warrant: they skip the step that builds structure → backing: the mechanism → qualifier: with daily use → rebuttal: one slow loaf is not the problem.

frameworks.name: Rogerian
frameworks.pairsWith: I Was Wrong, Five-Stage Spine; a softer partner for Myth – Truth – Proof.
frameworks.summary: Argue by common ground: state the other side so fairly they would sign it, show where it is right, find the shared goal, then make your case.
steps: State the other side so fairly they would sign it
Where it is right
The common ground: the goal you share
Your position, and how it serves that goal better
What changes if they take it
frameworks.whenToUse: Hostile or divided audiences, topics where parents feel judged. Wins fewer arguments and more people than refutation.
frameworks.example: Shortcuts save time while you cook, and that's true → the goal we share is a loaf worth the wait → fifteen minutes of folding gives both → here is what a week of it looks like.

frameworks.name: PASTOR
frameworks.pairsWith: Three-Act Revelation, I Was Wrong.
frameworks.summary: Problem, Amplify, Story and solution, Transformation, Offer, Response.
steps: Problem: name it in the audience's words
Amplify: what it costs if nothing changes
Story and solution: how it was solved
Transformation: the before and the after
Offer: what exactly they get
Response: the ask, one step
frameworks.whenToUse: Sales copy, launch emails, landing pages.
frameworks.example: The afternoons at the desk → the slump → the walk → the stretch → the routine matched to the week → start today.

frameworks.name: Problem – Agitate – Solve
frameworks.pairsWith: Pixar Pitch, Five-Stage Spine, Three-Act Revelation.
frameworks.summary: Name a problem the audience already feels, make the cost of leaving it real, then hand them the way out.
steps: Name the problem in the audience's own words
Agitate: what it costs them day to day if nothing changes
Show the solution and why it works
Proof: one concrete example, number or story
Call to action tied to the solution
frameworks.whenToUse: Pain-led topics where the audience knows the problem but not the fix.
frameworks.example: Your evenings lose to the phone every night → the whole evening is a wreck → a ten-minute wind-down that ends the scroll → what it did for one reader this week → save this for tonight.

frameworks.name: Before – After – Bridge
frameworks.pairsWith: Pixar Pitch, I Was Wrong.
frameworks.summary: Paint where they are, where they could be, and the bridge between the two.
steps: Before: their current situation, specific and recognisable
After: what it looks like once it is solved
Bridge: the steps that get them there
Call to action that starts the bridge
frameworks.whenToUse: Transformations and routines, where the payoff is easy to picture.
frameworks.example: Morning rush in tears → the morning as the calmest part of the day → three small changes in order → try step one tonight.

frameworks.name: Hook – Story – Offer
frameworks.pairsWith: Five-Stage Spine, Three-Act Revelation, I Was Wrong.
frameworks.summary: Stop the scroll, earn trust with a short first-person story, then make the ask.
steps: Hook: a pattern interrupt in the first line
Story: one moment with a turning point, told in first person
Lesson: what the story taught, in one sentence
Offer: the next step, product or follow
frameworks.whenToUse: Personal-brand content and anything where credibility comes from lived experience.
frameworks.example: "I almost quit running" → the lesson that changed how I train → what I do now → join the next run.

frameworks.name: Deliver, Then Tease
frameworks.pairsWith: Two Loops, Five-Stage Spine, Backwards Reveal.
frameworks.summary: Give one complete payoff, open a real second question that matters more, stop before it closes, and say where it continues.
steps: Deliver one complete thing: an exercise, an answer, a result the viewer can use today
Open a second question, real and bigger than the first
Stop before it closes
The ask: where the answer is (the app, the full video, the next post)
frameworks.whenToUse: Promos for a product, a course or a longer video. A cut that holds back the payoff it promised makes people angry at the ask; one that delivered first makes the ask welcome.
frameworks.example: One stretch, shown in full → "the next part is what to do when your back starts to ache" → cut → the week-by-week plan is in the full video, linked on the profile.

frameworks.name: Myth – Truth – Proof
frameworks.pairsWith: Any narrative shape; Backwards Reveal and I Was Wrong especially.
frameworks.summary: Take a belief the audience holds, grant the honest case for it, overturn it, and back the new view with evidence.
steps: State the common belief as people say it
Grant the honest case for it — validate before you reframe
Where it breaks
What is actually true
Proof from experience, research or the comments
What to do instead
frameworks.whenToUse: Contrarian and educational angles; comment-heavy topics. Validating first is what keeps the comments from turning on you.
frameworks.example: "Strength training is only for the young" → why people believe it → the study everyone misquotes → what supervised strength work does → three rules anyone can use.
